common_name: BabyWing Pink Begonia (Compact Orchid-Flowered Interspecific Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade or sun; BabyWing Pink is a compact interspecific hybrid begonia bearing large, orchid-like pink flowers on a tidy 12-15 inch plant.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial to full shade or sun, watering to keep soil evenly moist without becoming soggy. BabyWing Pink, an interspecific hybrid bred by PanAmerican Seed, bears unusually large, soft pink, orchid-like flowers held above glossy dark green foliage on a compact, well-branched plant, sharing the same smaller-scale growth habit as its sibling BabyWing White. It blooms nonstop from planting through frost with no deadheading required, holding up well to summer heat and humidity, and performs equally well in a shaded bed, a partly sunny border, or a container. It is essentially maintenance-free once established, needing only regular watering during dry spells; treat as an annual outside its tender perennial zone range.

common_name: Whopper Rose Bronze Leaf Begonia (Large-Leaved Vigorous Landscape Begonia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade or sun; a large-scale interspecific hybrid begonia bred for landscape mass planting.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial to full shade or sun, watering to keep soil evenly moist without becoming soggy. Whopper Rose Bronze Leaf bears large clusters of rose-pink flowers over glossy bronze-tinted foliage on a vigorous, sizable plant considerably larger than standard wax begonias, part of the interspecific hybrid group bred for bold landscape impact in mass plantings, large containers, or as a filler among taller shade perennials. It blooms nonstop from planting through frost with no deadheading required and tolerates summer heat and humidity better than many older bedding begonia types. It is essentially maintenance-free once established, needing only regular watering during dry spells; treat as an annual outside its tender perennial zone range.

common_name: Illumination Begonia (Trailing Tuberous Hanging Basket Begonia)

planting.note: Start tubers indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost or plant started nursery plants outdoors after frost danger has passed in a shaded hanging basket or container; Illumination is a trailing tuberous begonia series bred specifically for hanging displays.

directions: Grow in a hanging basket or elevated container filled with rich, well-drained, evenly moist potting mix in shade to partial shade. Illumination is a trailing tuberous begonia series bred to cascade rather than grow upright, producing large, fully double, rose-form flowers along long trailing stems that spill attractively over the edge of a basket through summer into fall. Unlike upright tuberous begonias, the trailing habit needs no staking, though the heavy bloom display benefits from a rich, consistently moist growing medium and regular light feeding. Cool nights and protection from harsh afternoon sun extend the bloom season and prevent the large flowers from fading quickly. Where winters are too cold to leave tubers in the ground, lift and store them dry over winter for replanting the following spring.

common_name: Nonstop Fire Begonia (Compact Upright Orange-Red Tuberous Begonia)

planting.note: Start tubers indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost or plant started nursery plants outdoors after frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained soil or containers in shade to partial shade.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or containers in shade to partial shade. Nonstop Fire bears fully double, rose-form flowers in a vivid orange-red on a compact, upright plant that blooms continuously from early summer through fall, part of the long-popular Nonstop series bred for reliable, weather-resistant bloom without the leggy stretch of older tuberous begonia strains. Its dense, mounded habit performs well in both garden beds and containers, and the flowers hold up better in rain and heat than many other double-flowered begonias. Where winters are too cold to leave tubers in the ground, lift and store them dry over winter for replanting the following spring.

common_name: Little Brother Montgomery Rex Begonia (Whorled Dark-Leaf Silver-Spiral Rex Begonia)

planting.note: Grow year-round as a houseplant or shaded patio container plant in bright, indirect light; move outdoors to a shaded spot for summer only after night temperatures stay reliably above 50°F.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, keeping soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, since Rex begonia rhizomes rot quickly in soggy conditions. Little Brother Montgomery is a long-cultivated Rex begonia cultivar named for the New Orleans blues pianist, bearing dark, near-black leaves marked with a distinctive silver spiral pattern radiating from the leaf center, a striking foliage display grown for the leaves rather than the plant's inconspicuous flowers. Like other Rex begonias it prefers higher humidity than typical houseplants and benefits from being grouped with other humidity-loving plants or set on a pebble tray. Outdoors in the Gulf South it can spend summer in a shaded patio container but should come indoors well before the first fall frost, since it has little cold tolerance. Divide the rhizome when repotting to propagate additional plants.

common_name: Black Fang Rex Begonia (Elongated Dark Pointed-Leaf Rex Begonia)

planting.note: Grow year-round as a houseplant or shaded patio container plant in bright, indirect light; move outdoors to a shaded spot for summer only after night temperatures stay reliably above 50°F.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, keeping soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, since Rex begonia rhizomes rot quickly in soggy conditions. Black Fang bears narrow, elongated, sharply pointed leaves in a deep near-black color, a departure from the broader, more rounded leaf shapes of most Rex begonia cultivars and one that gives the plant a spiky, dramatic silhouette in a mixed foliage display. Like other Rex begonias it prefers higher humidity than typical houseplants and benefits from being grouped with other humidity-loving plants or set on a pebble tray. Outdoors in the Gulf South it can spend summer in a shaded patio container but should come indoors well before the first fall frost, since it has little cold tolerance. Divide the rhizome when repotting to propagate additional plants.

Ricinifolia is a large, old-fashioned rhizomatous begonia species prized for its bold, deeply lobed, star-shaped leaves that resemble castor bean (Ricinus) foliage in outline, a much bigger and coarser-textured leaf than most rhizomatous Rex-type hybrids, on thick, hairy petioles arising from a stout above-ground rhizome. Its scale and bold texture make it a good specimen for a large shaded container or conservatory planting, standing out among finer-textured shade companions. Sprays of small pink flowers appear on tall stems in winter to early spring. Repot and divide the thick rhizome when it outgrows its container to propagate additional plants.

common_name: Maphil Begonia (Cathedral Begonia, Star-Shaped Green-and-Yellow Rhizomatous Begonia)

planting.note: Grow year-round as a houseplant or shaded patio container plant in bright, indirect light; move outdoors to a shaded spot for summer only after night temperatures stay reliably above 50°F.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, keeping soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, since Rex-type begonia rhizomes rot quickly in soggy conditions. Maphil, commonly sold as the Cathedral begonia, bears star-shaped, puckered, glossy leaves in bright chartreuse-yellow with dark green veins radiating outward, a bold, star-patterned variegation that has made it one of the more widely recognized rhizomatous begonia cultivars in the houseplant trade. Like other Rex-type begonias it prefers higher humidity than typical houseplants and benefits from being grouped with other humidity-loving plants or set on a pebble tray. Outdoors in the Gulf South it can spend summer in a shaded patio container but should come indoors well before the first fall frost, since it has little cold tolerance. Divide the rhizome when repotting to propagate additional plants.
